item.title: A clinical file format that says what it doesn’t know
item.dc:creator: Luis Garbayo
item.content:encoded:
Four design decisions behind .uos, an open container for dental 3D data, and what it deliberately does not claim.

A dental case usually arrives as three loose things: one or two STL files from an intraoral scanner, a folder with hundreds of DICOM slices from a CBCT, and a PDF report. Each one has its own coordinate system and opens in its own program. How they relate to each other, where this CBCT sits relative to this scan or which tooth a finding refers to, lives in the head of whoever looked at them, or inside proprietary software. It doesn’t travel with the data.

During an ANFAIA summer grant, with HISTORA and under the mentoring of Matías Molinas and Ismael Faro, I built UOS (Unified Oral Scene): an open container that carries those files plus the relationships between them. I told the story of the grant in a separate post. This one is about four decisions I would defend, and about what the format refuses to claim.

1. A ZIP that refuses to compress

A .uos is an uncompressed ZIP (STORE only) whose first entry is manifest.json. Uncompressed because the payloads are already compressed, and because it lets a client read the index at the end of the file, a few KB, and fetch a single asset with HTTP range requests instead of downloading the whole case. A real case with a CBCT is hundreds of megabytes, and the viewer’s README reports 299 MB for the one it was developed against. Reading a single asset should cost a small fraction of that.

The reference viewer (a TypeScript reader I wrote) is strict about this, and I checked each rule against its code before writing this. The strictness is the interesting part:

  • If manifest.json is not the first physical entry, it fails. That is the positive identification of the format. A file extension proves nothing.
  • If the server answers 200 to a range request instead of 206, it fails. The caller would believe it is downloading a 4 KB index and be downloading the whole container, and you would only notice on the bill.
  • ZIP64 is detected and declared unsupported. Reading a container over 4 GB with 32-bit fields would give truncated offsets, entries pointing into the middle of another file, and no error.

2. The reference exporter declares acquired data instead of carrying it

The container does not include the original scan or the DICOM series. It lists them as external assets, identified by their sha256 content address, and for the CBCT with one hash per slice. Whoever holds the original can prove it is the one that was measured. The container does not pretend to be one more copy of the patient record.

The Python test suite checks that the hashes mean something: one test removes a slice, another adds an extra one, another alters one, and each has to invalidate the series. The viewer’s own tests, which count the bytes requested and require that reading one asset costs a fraction of the container, only run when real containers are supplied. Those are clinical data and are not versioned, so on a fresh clone they skip. One precision, because it matters: this is the policy of the reference exporter. The format itself admits both included and external payloads.

3. Relationships come with their error and with who checked

The intraoral scan is the canonical frame. The CBCT lives in another frame, and a 4x4 matrix joins them together with its registration error. A field called verified_by holds who checked it. When it is null the validator warns that the registration is provisional, and the viewer labels it ‘sin verificar’ (unverified). An automatic registration nobody has reviewed and one signed off by a person are not the same thing, and the format refuses to let them look the same.

4. Whatever came from a model lives in one removable place

Everything inferred lives under derived/, with a sidecar that declares which model produced it, which version, and the hash of its weights. Its status is investigational, and on purpose. The hard rule: a .uos without derived/ is still valid and complete. The validator enforces the other direction too: anything declared as inferred (layer 3) outside derived/ is an error.

One consequence I liked. The tooth labels (FDI codes) are not baked into the scene file, even though the spec suggests that route for picking. If they were, deleting derived/ would stop deleting the inference, silently. A rule like this only holds if you refuse the convenient exception.

What it does not do

  • It does not validate anything clinically. The intended-use sheet is a draft to be ratified with a specialist, and it lists diagnosis, treatment planning and measuring bone or roots on the combined scene as out of scope.
  • It is not a standard. It is a container proposal with a published schema and a validator, and until someone else implements a reader it is only that.
  • The reference viewer implements loading, semantic picking and manual viewing without inference. The mesh pass, the volume pass, synchronized MPR and overlays are not implemented, and the README says exactly which is which.
  • Numbering teeth on real scans remains the weakest stage of the project. The format isolates it. It does not fix it.

Code: github.com/ANFAIA/Agentic-Smart-Health (Apache 2.0) and github.com/lgarbayo/uos-viewer (MIT). If you write a reader and it breaks on something, I want to know what.
